w: Session 5 has two parts, both by Dr. Litz. Furcation Management is his recorded lecture, which the Oct 15 quiz covered. Resective Osseous Surgery he taught in person on Oct 15, after the quiz; that class also went back over the furcation points he cares about most. Furcation vs. furcation defect A furcation is the normal spot on a tooth with more than one root (premolars and molars) where the roots split apart. Every such tooth has one. A furcation defect is what gum disease does to it: the gum and bone between the roots get destroyed, and attachment is lost down into that space. The single most important point of the lecture, repeated again and again: once gum disease reaches the furcation, the tooth's outlook drops sharply. Furcations are very hard for us to clean and even harder for patients, so look for them at every exam, cleaning and maintenance visit. Words to know, and the root trunk The root trunk is the solid part of the root from the CEJ (where enamel meets root) down to where the roots first split. The separate roots below it are also called root cones. The root complex is the whole root, trunk plus cones. The fornix is the roof of the furcation, and divergence is how far apart the roots spread, in millimeters. About 30% of a molar's attachment is on the root trunk and 70% on the separate roots. A short root trunk is a risk: if the trunk is only 2 mm long, 2 mm of attachment loss already opens the furcation. A long root trunk protects at first, because it takes much more loss to reach the furcation. But once the furcation is reached, a long trunk is bad news: these teeth usually can't have a root removed, and since a long trunk means short roots, there's little support left by then. Where the furcation openings are He called these numbers very important (from a 1979 study by Bower), measured down from the CEJ. On the upper first molar, which has three openings: the front (mesial) one about 3.6 mm down, the cheek-side (buccal) one about 4.2 mm, and the back (distal) one about 4.8 mm. Another slide rounds these to about 3.5, 4 and 5 mm. On the lower first molar, which has two: cheek side about 2.4 mm and tongue side about 2.5 mm. Those are much shallower, so a 4-5 mm pocket on a lower molar may already mean an open furcation. (The class exam-review guide gives the upper numbers as 3, 3.5 and 5 mm; same order.) On upper molars, the cheek-side opening is usually the narrowest, because the two cheek-side roots sit close together. The first molar's root trunk is usually shorter than the second molar's. Lower molars tilt toward the tongue, which puts the tongue-side opening a little deeper than the cheek side (a slide also gives it as more than 4 mm down and more than 0.75 mm wide). The lower molar's front root is wide cheek-to-tongue and pinched in the middle like an hourglass or kidney bean, with grooves facing the furcation. Upper premolars have two roots about 40% of the time, with the split about 8 mm down: a long trunk with short roots. The upper first premolar always has a groove on its front (mesial) surface (about 0.5 mm deep) next to the furcation, which floss slides right past even when used well. Why furcations are so hard to clean 81% of furcation openings are under 1 mm wide and 58% are under 0.75 mm, but a curette blade is 0.75-1.10 mm wide. So most of the time the blade simply doesn't fit, no matter how good the numbing, the time or the instrument; even thin ultrasonic tips struggle. His extracted molar showed it: the rounded outer root was smooth as glass, while inside the furcation, after several deep cleanings, tartar and inflamed tissue remained. Rounded (convex) surfaces are easy to clean; hollowed (concave) ones are much harder. The root surfaces facing into the furcation usually have dips. On the upper first molar, the front cheek-side root has a 0.3 mm dip 94% of the time, the back cheek-side root a 0.1 mm dip 31% of the time, and the palate root a 0.1 mm dip 17% of the time. The lower first molar is worse: the front root has a 0.7 mm dip every time, and the back root a 0.5 mm dip 99% of the time. During a deep cleaning you can't see these, and patients have almost no chance of cleaning them daily. Which furcations are affected most Teeth with short root trunks get furcation problems after only a little attachment loss, and usually do worse than single-rooted teeth. Upper molars are affected more often than lower molars. On upper molars, the cheek-side furcation is affected most, then the front one, then the back one. On lower molars, the cheek-side furcation is affected most. What causes it, and what makes it worse The main cause is ongoing attachment loss from gum disease, which comes from plaque. He expects that question on every perio exam and on boards. Other things add to it: How long the root trunk is, which affects both whether the furcation gets involved and which treatments are possible. Root shape: curved or fluted roots are easier to puncture during a root canal, which can cause furcation problems. How far apart the roots are: roots that sit close together or are fused keep instruments out; widely spread roots are easier to treat. Cervical enamel projections (CEPs): below. Enamel pearls: little balls of enamel, most often in molar furcations. Gum tissue can't attach to enamel, and the bump holds plaque. On an x-ray, a white half-circle in the furcation suggests one. Small ones can be ground off, usually after opening the gum. Dental work: a filling or crown edge that overhangs near a furcation traps plaque and leads to bone and attachment loss. Edges below the gumline should stay inside the gum pocket. Intermediate bifurcation ridge: a rounded ridge of root surface running front-to-back across the furcation opening of a lower molar, joining the two roots. It leaves a domed hollow above it that traps plaque where no one can reach once it's exposed. Cervical enamel projections He called these a definite test question, and something to know for life. A CEP is a thin, pointed strip of enamel reaching down from the CEJ toward or into the furcation, like a widow's peak. It happens when enamel formation doesn't stop before the root starts forming. Because gum tissue can't attach to enamel, the gum just lies on top of it, and the CEP acts like a funnel steering plaque straight into the furcation. CEPs show up on about 30% of lower molars and 15% of upper molars, more often on second molars and on the cheek side. They're graded by how far down they reach: Grade 1: the CEJ clearly dips down toward the furcation. Grade 2: the enamel gets close to the furcation but doesn't enter it. Grade 3: the enamel reaches into the furcation. The key fact for treatment: new attachment won't form on enamel. If there's no bone or attachment loss, often the case with Grades 1 and 2, usually leave it and watch it. If there is loss, remove the CEP. Thin enamel comes off with a diamond or finishing bur (usually after opening the gum, sometimes without if it's very shallow). Thicker enamel can be removed carefully without reaching the nerve, and on a living tooth, warn the patient it may be sensitive to hot and cold. His bigger rule: if one furcation is involved in a mouth that's otherwise healthy, look for a CEP. One deep spot on one tooth means something about that tooth is different: a CEP, an overhang, leftover cement, or a cracked root under a root canal. Grading furcations Furcations are checked with the curved Nabers probe, slid gently under the gum to feel for the opening; it takes seconds. The Glickman grades (1953), the system he uses: Grade I: early. You can feel the opening, but the bone between the roots is intact and the probe can't hook in. Grade II: some bone between the roots is gone, but not all the way through. The probe hooks in and catches when pulled up. Grade III: all the way through; the probe goes in one side and out the other. Grade IV: all the way through, and the gum has pulled back so you can see through it. The Hamp system (1975), common among periodontists, uses millimeters of sideways loss: degree 1, under 3 mm in; degree 2, more than 3 mm but not through; degree 3, all the way through. Both Glickman and Hamp measure sideways (horizontal) loss. Tarnow and Fletcher (1984) add the up-and-down (vertical) depth in steps of 3 mm: A, 0-3 mm; B, 4-6 mm; C, 7 mm or more. Deeper means a worse outlook. Finding them: probing and x-rays The cheek-side opening of upper molars and both openings of lower molars are easy to reach. On upper molars, the front (mesiopalatal) opening sits toward the palate, so probe it from the palate side. The back (distopalatal) opening sits about halfway across, so it can be probed from either side. On x-rays, bone loss in a furcation can come from gum disease, a root canal infection, a punctured root or bite trauma. Lower molars, with two roots, show it clearly. Upper molars are harder because roots overlap on the film: bone loss at the cheek-side furcation is often hidden behind the palate root. Loss at the front or back openings often shows as a furcation arrow, a small dark triangle pointing into the furcation. About 30-55% of Grade II or III furcations show one. If you see an arrow, a furcation problem is very likely, but many don't show one, so an arrow must never be the only test. His rule for all of dentistry: examine the patient first, reach a diagnosis, then use x-rays to confirm it. Take both periapical x-rays and vertical bitewings. In one study (Ross and Thompson, 1980), the clinical exam alone found furcation problems in only 3% of upper and 9% of lower molars; adding x-rays raised that to 65% of upper but only 23% of lower molars. Use both. Deciding whether to treat Just having a furcation involved doesn't automatically mean it needs treatment. Active gum disease and anything nearby that's making it worse decide that. Removing plaque and tartar is always the most important step, but the cause also has to go: leave a CEP, an overhang or leftover tartar, and the loss continues. Early furcation problems usually need no treatment unless there's a local cause you can fix. Moderate to advanced ones have a lot of sideways loss; the aim is an area the patient and hygienist can keep clean, and the best long-term approach is to shrink or get rid of the furcation. Treatment has two goals: 1. get the plaque off the exposed root surfaces, and 2. leave a shape the patient can clean. Without surgery: deep cleaning (Phase I), antibiotics placed in the pocket after cleaning (a later lecture), and reshaping the tooth at the furcation opening (furcation plasty). With surgery: opening the gum to clean, making a tunnel, regrowing bone (regeneration), removing a root, or pulling the tooth and placing an implant. By class: Class I, deep cleaning, fixing local causes and smoothing the opening. Class II, smoothing the opening, regrowing bone (GTR), removing a root, or extraction. Class III, a tunnel, removing a root, or extraction. Whether a tooth is worth treating also depends on how bad the furcation is (Class I and shallow Class II do better), how much support is left around the whole tooth, pocket depths, looseness, root canal problems, the bite, how useful the tooth is (a lower molar with nothing biting against it may not be worth saving), the patient's health, and their brushing and flossing. Nothing works if the patient can't keep it clean. Surgical options The simplest is opening a gum flap to clean: cuts around the teeth and lifting the gum and its lining give a view in. If the bone loss is sideways only, not straight down, a thorough cleaning often calms the inflammation and shrinks the pocket. Reshaping the tooth (odontoplasty: removing a CEP, smoothing a ridge) or the bone (osteoplasty) makes the furcation shallower and easier to clean. Regrowing bone needs the right patient and tooth. Poor candidates: uncontrolled diabetes, a weak immune system, smoking, or poor home care. The best teeth are lower molars and the cheek-side furcation of upper molars, at degree II. The front and back furcations of upper molars are much harder because they're hard to reach. At degree III, regrowing bone does no better than ordinary surgery. Things in its favor: thicker gums, no gum recession, and higher bone between the teeth. Roots sitting very close can get in the way; a previous root canal does not rule it out. The steps: open the gum, clean the root thoroughly (without this nothing grows back), remove any enamel projections or pearls, pack in bone graft and/or cover it with a membrane held by a dissolving sling stitch, close the gum over it, and no brushing or flossing there for up to 4 weeks (chlorhexidine rinse instead). About a year later, an x-ray shows whether bone filled in. Tunneling purposely removes bone to open the furcation all the way through, creating a Glickman Grade IV on purpose, so the patient can push a small brush through. It's for deep Class II and Class III, and only on lower molars with long, well-spread roots. The catch: cavities in tunneled molars are common, since root surfaces decay fast. It's rarely done now that implants exist. Root resection (root amputation) cuts off one or more roots where they meet the furcation, keeping the crown and the other roots. The root removed most often is the back cheek-side (distobuccal) root of the upper first molar. It's for deep Class II and Class III, gets rid of the furcation, and means the patient also needs a root canal and new dental work. It's still used, for example when a lower molar holding up a bridge (already root-canal treated) cracks one root while the other is sound: remove the cracked root and keep the bridge. Hemisection removes a root plus the part of the crown above it, usually on lower molars, making a two-rooted tooth into a one-rooted one. Implants have made it much rarer: it takes a root canal specialist, then the periodontist, then the restorative dentist, over many costly visits. The order for removing a root: the root canal first, with the opening filled directly with amalgam or composite; a temporary crown; then separating and removing the root, without exposing the bone between the roots, leaving bits of the furcation roof, punching into the canals, or leaving sharp corners; then gum surgery to remove bone defects around the remaining roots, keeping the temporary crown's edges at least 3 mm above the bone; and finally the permanent crown or bridge, on a rigid framework and with a bite that keeps sideways forces low. In class: the furcation points he repeated Before the new topic, Dr. Litz went back over the recorded lecture. Every molar has a furcation; the trouble is a furcation defect, and once gum disease reaches the furcation the tooth's outlook drops sharply, because we can barely clean it and the patient almost never can. He asked again for the opening depths ("I want you to know these numbers"): upper first molar front-palate side 3.6, cheek side 4.2, back-palate side 4.8 mm; lower molar cheek side 2.4 and tongue side 2.5 mm. So when a molar probes 4, 5 or 6 mm, assume a furcation is already open. Most openings are narrower than a curette blade, and the root walls inside the furcation are dented inward, which hides tartar. Upper molars break down partly because their bone is less dense and the cheek-side bone is thin. A thin enamel projection usually comes off with a finishing bur in light strokes; warn the patient about cold sensitivity if it's thick. One deep spot in an otherwise healthy mouth means something is wrong with that one tooth: an enamel projection, an overhanging filling, leftover cement, or a cracked root on a root-canal-treated molar, which means the tooth comes out. He checks every molar with a curved Nabers probe and uses the Glickman grades, as the school does. Phase I, the recheck, and when surgery comes in In gum care, Phase I is home-care teaching (always first), a deep cleaning, fixing things that trap plaque (overhanging fillings, open contacts, reshaping enamel projections, which often can only be reached in surgery), and the recheck. Phase II is surgery, followed by regular maintenance visits. Phase I calms the inflammation, shrinks pockets that were only deep because the gum was swollen, firms up the tissue so it bleeds less and holds together in surgery, and above all aims for a mouth the patient can keep clean. He repeats that goal constantly: we clean their teeth a few times a year; they clean them 700 to 800 times. That's why a patient can't skip the deep cleaning even if they'll need surgery: a surgeon treats an infected cut before operating on the broken bone under it, and swollen gum bleeds and tears. The recheck comes 4 to 6 weeks after Phase I, when the cleaning has had its full effect and home care is at its best. It asks whether the first round of treatment is done (causes controlled, good home care, no plaque or tartar, less inflammation, shallower pockets), whether what's left can be maintained, and whether surgery would help: bone reshaping, regrowing bone, an open-flap cleaning or a gum graft. Three outcomes: shallow pockets and good home care means maintenance every 3 to 4 months; plaque and bleeding everywhere means repeat Phase I; good home care but pockets still too deep for a brush or floss means surgery. His slides list 11 reasons for gum surgery, led by getting access to clean the roots and getting rid of pockets. A 1981 study he still uses showed that the deeper the pocket, the more tartar a deep cleaning leaves behind: in 3 to 5 mm pockets failure becomes more likely, and over 5 mm it dominates. Deeper pockets have more root to clean, more irregular spots (like furcations), and a narrow bottom you can't reach. Lifting the gum lets you see what you're doing, like doing a filling with your eyes open. Bone surgery: why remove bone The goal of osseous surgery is to get rid of pockets and leave a shallow gum collar the patient can keep clean. Healthy gum is scalloped, like a child's drawing of ocean waves: higher between the teeth, lower in the middle of each tooth. It goes back to that shape after surgery even if the bone underneath doesn't. His most important slide: if the bone doesn't follow the shape of the gum above it, the pockets come back. So the surgery reshapes the bone to match. Treating bone loss by removing bone sounds backwards, but sometimes you fight fire with fire. Gum disease leaves the bone edge uneven. In health, the bone between teeth sits about 1 to 2 mm below the enamel line on an X-ray, and it sits higher than the bone on the cheek and tongue sides, following the curve of the enamel line. That's positive architecture, the goal. In negative (reverse) architecture the bone between the teeth sits lower, making a crater with deep pockets; flat is in between. When getting to positive would mean removing too much bone, he settles for flat rather than weaken the tooth. The cost is small: about 0.6 mm of supporting bone height on average. Bone comes off the cheek and tongue sides, never between the teeth, because those narrower surfaces hold less of the tooth's support. Teeth feel a bit looser afterward but settle back within about a year. When to do it, and when not to Bone surgery fits when the deep cleaning didn't stop the disease; pockets stayed deep after cleaning, especially around furcations; bone loss is mild to moderate and even; there are shallow bone craters or shallow 1-, 2- or 3-wall holes; a shallow furcation needs opening up; or there are bony ledges and bumps (like tori) where the gum meets the tooth at almost a right angle. The aim is bone that tapers to a thin edge at the root, with rounded rather than dented shapes. It's ruled out by poor home care (the big one; surgery cures nothing, it only makes cleaning possible), a patient who won't follow the plan (like wanting to skip the deep cleaning), shallow pockets (surgery there causes attachment loss), a bone hole that could be regrown instead (Session 6), a result that would look bad (long front teeth with a high smile), and uncontrolled medical disease. Ostectomy, osteoplasty and the steps Ostectomy removes bone that supports the tooth (bone the ligament attaches to). Osteoplasty only reshapes bone that isn't attached to the tooth, so it can be thinned more freely. The steps: 1. vertical grooves between the teeth, 2. blending over the roots, 3. flattening the bone between the teeth, and 4. tapering the bone edge, the careful ostectomy on the cheek and tongue sides. The most important step of all is cleaning the roots thoroughly: if the roots aren't clean, nothing works. On upper molars, each cheek-side root is treated like its own tooth, and the bone in the furcation is never removed: exposing it lowers the outlook, and it's hard to get back. Silk stitches come out after a week. Patients should expect longer-looking teeth, some cold sensitivity on the exposed roots, and wider gaps that catch food but can now be cleaned with a small brush. In his case, a bridge the patient couldn't clean under became cleanable with an interproximal brush six months after surgery, the whole point. But if the patient doesn't clean, none of it works.
